title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — September 21, 2026 (A Bangladesh Ruling Cuts Both Ways, and a Delisted Company Is Still Ranked)
headline: Bangladesh's tribunal ordered death sentences and victim-asset seizures in the same September 15 ruling.
summary:
Ten organizations were checked overnight. Zero score-change proposals were filed, and zero scores changed on the public record. Six readings confirmed the published score within normal range; four raised open questions serious enough to flag for further review rather than close quietly.

Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced seven former officials to death in absentia on September 15 for the 2024 crackdown that killed at least 1,400 protesters, and in the same ruling ordered half of five convicted men's assets seized and paid to victims' families. A new research measurement weighed both facts on their own terms: the compensation order and a first-ever state admission of the violence pull one way; arrests with no evidence threshold and trials with no chosen defense lawyer, a Human Rights Watch finding from July, pull the other. The two effects offset almost exactly, producing a reading of 35.0 out of 100, a decline of 4.8 points from the published 39.8 — inside the confirmation range, but the third consecutive independent read at that level, now flagged for a calibration check rather than filed as a change. No one has been executed, and 64 of the 68 people convicted in the proceedings remain outside the country.

A Russian missile and drone strike killed five people and injured 35 in Kyiv on September 8. Because the attack is Russian conduct, it produces no change to Ukraine's own score. What the strike did surface is Ukraine's own capacity: its emergency service reported casualties within hours across four regions, a functioning response chain — but Kyiv had only one certified public bomb shelter as of September 3, funded privately, and the law requiring shelters in new buildings only took effect the day of the strike. Those facts sit just outside this review's evidence window and are logged as watch items rather than scored.

A United Nations Human Rights Council fact-finding mission reported on September 17 that Iran's 2025–26 protest crackdown killed people in all 31 provinces, killed at least 221 children including one as young as two, and executed at least 29 men after rushed trials — calling the pattern "widespread and systematic." Iran's score, already near the benchmark's floor at 2.5 out of 100, does not move: the evidence behind it is now backed by a United Nations mandate rather than watchdog counts alone, but a move to the benchmark's absolute floor needs two independent high-tier sources, and tonight there is one.

CenterPoint Energy told securities regulators on September 14 that hackers stole customer personal data; an unverified hacker claim of 7.49 million affected records was excluded because no one has confirmed it. Alphabet/Google was checked against the same antitrust suit that produced zero movement for three AI labs a cycle earlier, and produced the same result, holding at 40.0 — a score that already sits exactly on the line between two of the benchmark's tiers. Oakland's first individually researched score confirmed after establishing that one of three people named in a federal fraud indictment is a federal aviation inspector, not a city employee — the two Oakland Police Department pilots involved are accused of faking flight-certification tests on their own account, not on department orders, while Oakland's police force separately reached full compliance with a 23-year-old federal oversight order for the first time.

A routine re-check of Macy's produced a reading that would cross Macy's from its published Functional tier into Developing — but the reading was not filed, because it traces almost entirely to one researcher reading the same public record 0.15 points differently than a documented assessment on file from five months ago, with zero new evidence found in this review's window. Marsh & McLennan, ranked 42nd of 447 companies on a score nobody has ever individually researched, produced an indicative first-pass reading 24.6 points lower — also not filed, because two independent raters disagree with it and the company's own sustainability report was not read this cycle. And Key Energy Services, published in the Fortune 500 list with a score of 21.9, turns out to have deregistered from public reporting in December 2020; no score was issued, because assessing a company with no current public record would measure its silence, not its conduct.

Release watch: 0 sources registered — detection did not run.

topSignals.title: A Bangladesh Court Ruling Pulls the Benchmark in Two Directions at Once
topSignals.whyItMatters: Bangladesh's tribunal ordered death sentences and victim payouts in the same ruling. The benchmark measured both effects honestly instead of letting them cancel out silently.
topSignals.description:
On September 15, Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced seven former officials to death in absentia for their role in the 2024 protest crackdown that killed at least 1,400 people, according to the United Nations. In the same ruling, the tribunal ordered half of five convicted men's assets confiscated and paid to the families of those killed or injured — a real transfer of resources to victims, not a symbolic gesture.

The research measurement this cycle looked at both halves of that ruling on their own terms rather than netting them into a single number. Two areas moved up: Accountability and Equity, on the strength of the state prosecuting its own former leadership and ordering compensation. Two areas moved down: Empathy and Boundaries, because the death sentences were handed down in absentia, with a state-appointed lawyer rather than one the defendants chose, and Human Rights Watch found in July that prosecutors can order arrests "without meeting any evidential threshold."

The four moves happen to offset almost exactly, producing a reading of 35.0 out of 100 — the same figure two earlier independent reads produced, and 4.8 points below the published 39.8. That gap is under the benchmark's five-point threshold for a formal proposal, so nothing was filed; three matching reads in a row is instead flagged for a calibration check. No one has been executed, and 64 of the 68 people convicted in the proceedings remain outside the country, which is why the death sentences weigh on the score without dominating it.

evidence.quote: responsible for conduct including the incitement to and ordering of killings during the crackdown
evidence.claim: Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal found seven former officials responsible for ordering killings during the 2024 crackdown.

evidence.quote: ordered the confiscation of half the assets belonging to the five men, saying that they will be distributed as compensation to the families of those who died or were injured
Trials in absentia are held without appropriate safeguards, including defendants' right to choose lawyers to represent them.

topSignals.title: A UN Mission Confirms Iran's Crackdown Was "Widespread and Systematic"
topSignals.whyItMatters: A United Nations fact-finding mission found Iran killed people in all 31 provinces and executed dozens after rushed trials. Iran's near-floor score holds — the finding makes the case stronger, not different.
topSignals.description:
An Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran reported to the UN Human Rights Council on September 17 that Iran's 2025–26 crackdown on protesters amounted to crimes against humanity. The mission found security forces killed people in all 31 of Iran's provinces, that at least 221 children were killed, some as young as two, and that at least 29 men were executed between March and August 2026 after expedited trials, with more than 70 people — including three boys — still at risk of execution.

Iran already sits near the benchmark's absolute floor, at 2.5 out of 100, the third-lowest of 191 countries measured. That number does not move tonight. What changes is the strength of the evidence behind it: the case for 2.5 previously rested mainly on watchdog tallies, and now carries a United Nations mandate's own finding of crimes against humanity. A move all the way to the benchmark's zero floor was considered and set aside for now — the benchmark's own rule requires two independent high-tier sources before a floor designation, and this cycle located one.

evidence.quote: Iranian security forces carried out killings on a large scale in all 31 provinces
evidence.source: The National (reporting the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran)

evidence.quote: At least 221 children were reportedly killed, some of them as young as two years old
evidence.source: The National (reporting the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran)

evidence.quote: Murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians
evidence.source: The National (reporting the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran)

topSignals.title: A Company That Deregistered in 2020 Is Still Ranked in the Fortune 500
topSignals.whyItMatters: Key Energy Services stopped filing with securities regulators nearly six years ago. It has no public record left to measure — the fix is a catalogue correction, not a new score.
topSignals.description:
Key Energy Services filed a Form 15 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on December 14, 2020, deregistering from public reporting requirements after emerging from a 2016 bankruptcy and restructuring roughly 80% of its debt out of court. It has made no public SEC filing since. There is no annual report, no workforce data, no safety record and no sustainability disclosure to read for any period after 2020.

Key Energy Services is nonetheless published in the Fortune 500 index at position 500, carrying a score of 21.9 out of 100. Assessing 40 separate behaviors for a company with no current public record would measure its silence rather than its conduct, so no score was issued this cycle. The finding is about the benchmark's own catalogue, not about the company: the same class of problem the benchmark identified in August 2026, when it found Halodi Robotics and 1X Technologies were the same company listed twice. Until a decision is made about whether deregistered, privately held companies belong in the index at all, this entity is being set aside from further nightly review rather than resurfacing each cycle as an unscorable candidate.

evidence.claim: Key Energy Services filed a Form 15 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 14 December 2020, deregistering from public reporting requirements, and has made no public SEC filing since.

topSignals.title: A Reading That Would Cross a Tier Line Was Checked and Not Filed
topSignals.whyItMatters: A fresh look at Macy's produced a lower tier than its published score. It stayed unfiled because nothing new happened — one researcher read the same public record slightly differently.
topSignals.description:
Macy's published score of 41.3 out of 100 sits in the benchmark's Functional tier, 1.3 points above the line into the lower Developing tier. A routine rotation check this cycle found that this score is not an old placeholder — it traces to a full assessment on file from April 22, 2026, filed under a mangled filename that had made it look, incorrectly, like Macy's had never been individually researched.

Re-reading the same public record this cycle produced 37.5 out of 100, which would cross the line into Developing. That reading was not filed. The entire gap amounts to 0.15 points on a five-point scale — well within the range one researcher's reading can differ from another's on the same facts — and this review found zero new evidence about Macy's conduct in the two weeks it covers. Macy's did cut roughly 1,050 jobs and close 14 stores in 2026, filing the required 60-day notices in January; it also pays for a fully funded education benefit for every employee and negotiated severance of up to 52 weeks for unionized staff in California. None of that is new. Macy's published score stays at 41.3, and a single confirmed new finding about Macy's labor or customer conduct would be enough to make the tier question testable on evidence rather than re-reading.

evidence.claim: Macy's filed the required 60-day WARN notices on 12 and 13 January 2026 for warehouse and fulfillment layoffs effective mid-March.
A UFCW Local 5 contract for Macy's California workers added $1.50 an hour, a ratification bonus of up to $1,200, and severance of up to 52 weeks.

topSignals.title: The Highest-Ranked Unresearched Score in the Benchmark Gets a Closer Look
topSignals.whyItMatters: Marsh & McLennan sits 42nd of 447 companies on a score nobody has ever individually checked. A first look suggests it may be too high — which is exactly why it wasn't changed yet.
topSignals.description:
Seven of Marsh & McLennan's eight published dimension scores read an identical 3.5 out of 5, the fingerprint of a starting placeholder rather than a researched measurement. No individual assessment of the insurance and risk-advisory firm exists on file, despite its position at 42nd of 447 companies in the Fortune 500 index with a published composite of 60.9.

A short first pass — four searches, not a full 40-point review — produced an indicative reading 24.6 points lower, which would cross two tier lines. That reading was not filed and should not be read as a measurement: independent raters disagree with it (MSCI rates the firm AA, a leader grade, and Sustainalytics puts its risk at 19.5, both low-risk readings), and the company's own sustainability report was not read this cycle. What the pass did establish on the record: $187 million in restructuring costs, mostly severance, under a three-year program called Thrive, and a health-plan lawsuit the firm must now answer rather than having had dismissed. Marsh & McLennan is referred for a dedicated full assessment rather than a routine nightly check, the same treatment the benchmark gave a cluster of placeholder robotics-industry scores in August 2026.

evidence.claim: Marsh & McLennan incurred $187 million of restructuring costs, primarily severance, through March 31, 2026 under its three-year "Thrive" program.
Marsh & McLennan holds an MSCI ESG rating of AA (Leader) and a Sustainalytics risk score of 19.5 (low risk).
Marsh & McLennan must face a health-plan fiduciary-breach case rather than having it dismissed.

topSignals.title: Kyiv's Bomb-Shelter Gap Surfaces in a Strike That Isn't Ukraine's Score to Bear
topSignals.whyItMatters: Russia struck Kyiv on September 8; that's Russian conduct, not Ukraine's. What the strike revealed about Ukraine's own shelter gap is being tracked, not scored yet.
topSignals.description:
A Russian drone and missile attack killed five people and injured 35 in Kyiv on September 8, 2026, ending a brief ceasefire during a visit by US envoys to Moscow. Because the harm was inflicted by a foreign state at war with Ukraine, it produces no change to Ukraine's own score — the benchmark measures an institution's own conduct, and scoring a country down for being attacked would penalize the wrong actor.

What is scoreable is Ukraine's own response. Its State Emergency Service reported casualties through official channels within hours across four regions, and rescue crews reached trapped residents — a functioning alert-and-rescue chain. Physical shelter is thinner: as of September 3, five days before the strike, Kyiv had only one certified public modular shelter, funded by a private company rather than the state, after a summer of strikes that killed around 150 civilians in the city. A law requiring shelters in new construction took effect on September 8 — the day of the strike itself. Those facts fall just outside this review's evidence window and are logged as watch items rather than scored. Separately, and not examined this cycle, Ukraine's own human rights commissioner has called draft-enforcement abuses at recruitment centers "systematic and large-scale" — the most likely source of a future downward reading.

evidence.claim: Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported casualties through official channels within hours across Kyiv, Odesa, Mykolaiv and the Kyiv region after Russian strikes.

As of 3 September 2026, only one certified public modular shelter had been installed in Kyiv, funded by a private concrete manufacturer, after strikes killed around 150 civilians in the city over the summer.

topSignals.title: CenterPoint Told Regulators Customer Data Was Stolen — and What Wasn't Used
topSignals.whyItMatters: CenterPoint's own securities filing confirms a data breach. A hacker's unverified 7.49-million-record claim was excluded because no one has confirmed it.
topSignals.description:
CenterPoint Energy told the Securities and Exchange Commission on September 14, 2026 that "a portion of its customers' personal information was stolen in a data breach earlier this month" — the utility's own words, in its own regulatory filing. Five proposed federal class actions followed within days, filed by customers in Texas, Indiana and Minnesota; those remain allegations, untested in court.

A widely circulated figure claiming 7.49 million records were affected was not used anywhere in this assessment: it originates from the hacker's own claim, appears on an undated website, and CenterPoint has not confirmed it. This is CenterPoint's first individually researched score, produced without prior history to compare against. It measured 33.8 out of 100, 2.1 points below the published 35.9 — inside the benchmark's normal confirmation range. The utility's income-based Gas Affordability Program, which credits charges above 6% of a household's annual income, is the strongest thing in the record; the weakest is that its own problems — the 2024 Hurricane Beryl outage failures, this breach, and a billing practice that applied payments to unregulated charges before regulated gas bills — have each surfaced through outsiders rather than the company's own monitoring.

evidence.quote: a portion of its customers' personal information was stolen in a data breach earlier this month
evidence.claim: CenterPoint Energy confirmed a customer data breach in a Form 8-K filed with the SEC.
evidence.source: HelpNet Security (reporting CenterPoint Energy's SEC Form 8-K)

evidence.claim: Five proposed federal class actions were filed against CenterPoint between 10 and 13 September 2026, pleading that the utility failed to maintain basic data security standards.

topSignals.title: One of Three 'Oakland Cops' Indicted Turns Out to Be a Federal Inspector
topSignals.whyItMatters: A federal indictment named three people as Oakland police; one is a federal FAA inspector. Correcting the record changed how the finding counts against the city.
topSignals.description:
A federal indictment unsealed on September 10, 2026 charged three people with conspiring to fake flight-certification tests for Oakland Police Department helicopter pilots between July 2023 and March 2024. One of the three, William Miller, is a Federal Aviation Administration safety inspector — a federal official, not a city employee — described in reporting as the person who made the scheme possible. Only two of the three, both OPD pilots, work for the city.

This review treats the fraud as the two pilots' own conduct rather than department policy: nothing in the public record suggests Oakland's police department directed or knew about the scheme. A real question does remain — city employees flew the city's police helicopter over a populated city on credentials that were allegedly faked, and no evidence either way was found on whether the department checks its own pilots' paperwork. That question is scored as an open supervision gap, not an established institutional failure.

Set against that: Oakland's police department became fully compliant with all 51 tasks required by a 23-year-old federal court oversight order for the first time ever, a federal monitor found in May 2026. A judge is due to decide on September 29 whether to end that oversight. Oakland's first individually researched score, 35.6 out of 100, confirms 0.3 points below the published 35.9.

evidence.quote: For the first time in the history of its federal court oversight, the Oakland Police Department has complied with all of its 51 mandated tasks

evidence.claim: William Miller, one of three defendants, is a Federal Aviation Administration safety inspector — a federal official, not an Oakland city employee.
Brandon Mart and David Mac allegedly conspired with the FAA inspector to obtain pilot certifications between July 2023 and March 2024 using fraudulent documents.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries — A Ruling That Cuts Both Ways, an Attack That Isn't the Target's Score, and a UN Finding That Changes Nothing and Everything
sectorAlerts.headline: Bangladesh, Ukraine and Iran all confirmed within normal range tonight, each for a different reason.
observations: Bangladesh (39.8 published, 35.0 measured): a tribunal ruling ordering both death sentences and victim compensation moved two areas up and two down by equal amounts, the third consecutive matching read.

Ukraine (50.0 published, 49.4 measured, carried): a Russian strike on Kyiv scores nothing against Ukraine; a near-absent public bomb-shelter supply is logged as a watch item outside this review's window.
Iran (2.5 published, 2.5 measured): a UN fact-finding mission corroborated the near-floor placement with a crimes-against-humanity finding, but a floor designation needs a second high-tier source.

sectorAlerts.sector: Fortune 500 — Two Findings Checked and Left Unfiled, and Two Organizations With Record Problems
sectorAlerts.headline: CenterPoint Energy and Alphabet confirmed on real evidence, while Macy's, Marsh & McLennan and Key Energy Services each surfaced a record-keeping problem instead of a clean score change.
observations: CenterPoint Energy (35.9 published, 33.8 measured, first individual score): the company's own SEC filing confirms a data breach; an unverified 7.49-million-record hacker claim was excluded entirely.
Alphabet/Google (40.0 published, 40.0 measured): held unchanged under the same antitrust-suit screening applied to three AI labs a cycle earlier; the score already sits exactly on a tier boundary.
Macy's (41.3 published, 37.5 measured, not filed): a re-reading of an existing April 2026 assessment would cross a tier line, but the entire gap is 0.15 points with zero new evidence found.

Marsh & McLennan (60.9 published, indicative 36.3, not filed): the highest-ranked company in the index without an individual assessment produced a first-pass reading 24.6 points lower, contradicted by two independent raters and referred for a dedicated study.

Key Energy Services (21.9 published, no score issued): deregistered from SEC reporting in December 2020 and has no current public record to assess; the finding is a catalogue problem, not a conduct problem.

observations: Oakland (35.9 published, 35.6 measured, first individual score): one of three people named in a fraud indictment is a federal FAA inspector, not an Oakland employee; the city's police department also reached full compliance with a 23-year-old federal oversight order for the first time.

sectorAlerts.sector: AI Labs — A Private Company's Silence Produces Most of a Large Gap
sectorAlerts.headline: Lightmatter's first individually researched score came in well below its placeholder value, almost entirely because a private company discloses almost nothing publicly.
observations: Lightmatter (37.5 published, 31.3 measured, first individual score, not filed): fifteen of forty measured behaviors were scored on the absence of published evidence rather than on documented conduct, a pattern likely to recur across other private companies in the same index.

methodologyNotes.name: A Ruling That Cuts Both Ways Doesn't Get Netted to Silence
methodologyNotes.description: Bangladesh's tribunal ordered both death sentences and victim compensation in a single ruling. Rather than letting the two effects cancel into an unremarked flat score, this cycle scored each direction on its own terms — two areas up, two down — and reported that they happened to offset, rather than treating an unchanged number as evidence that nothing happened.

methodologyNotes.name: A Score Attached to an Organization That No Longer Files Publicly Is Not a Measurement
methodologyNotes.description: Key Energy Services deregistered from SEC reporting in December 2020 and has no public record from any period since. Scoring it anyway would measure the absence of information, not the company's conduct, so no score was issued. The same reasoning applies to any other catalogue entry describing a company that has gone dark.

methodologyNotes.name: Re-Reading the Same Record Is Not New Evidence
methodologyNotes.description: A tier-crossing reading for Macy's this cycle traced to 0.15 points of difference between two researchers reading the same public record five months apart, with no new conduct found in between. The benchmark's rule is that a band crossing needs documented new evidence, not simply a second opinion on old evidence, so the finding was checked and left unfiled.

methodologyNotes.name: A Placeholder Cohort's Gap Is a Cohort Question Until It's Tested Cohort-Wide
methodologyNotes.description: Both Marsh & McLennan and Lightmatter produced large first-time gaps against shared placeholder starting values this cycle. In both cases, the gap traces to a pattern common across many other entries in the same placeholder group — disclosure absence for private companies, an unresearched flat seed value for a highly ranked firm — rather than to a documented finding unique to either company. Both are referred for a dedicated cohort study rather than an individual score change.
